lessons.title: What Needs Electricity?
objectives: Name things that use electricity
Sort devices into battery-powered and plug-in
explanation: Electricity is a kind of energy that makes things work: lights glow, fans spin, fridges stay cold and phones charge.
Some things get electricity from batteries — torches, toy cars, TV remotes. Others plug into sockets in the wall — fridges, washing machines, televisions.
Some things don't need electricity at all: a bicycle, a book or a ball!

vocabulary.meaning: energy that makes many machines work
the place in the wall where plugs go

examples: A torch uses batteries.
A fridge plugs into the wall.

story.title: The Day the Lights Went Out
story.text: One stormy evening, the power went off. The fan stopped and the lights went dark! Ivaan found his torch and switched it on — it still worked because it had batteries. Mama lit a candle, and they played board games, which didn't need electricity at all. When the lights came back, everyone cheered.

lessons.title: Safe With Electricity
objectives: State key rules for electrical safety
Explain why water and electricity are dangerous together
explanation: Electricity from wall sockets is very strong and can badly hurt people. Never put fingers or objects into sockets.
Water and electricity are dangerous together. Never touch switches or plugs with wet hands, and keep drinks away from devices.
If you see a broken wire, sparks or smell burning, don't touch — tell a grown-up straight away. Small batteries in toys are safe to use, but never put batteries in your mouth.

vocabulary.meaning: when electricity passes through the body and hurts it

examples: Drying hands before switching on a light.

story.title: Kiko's Wet Hands
story.text: Kiko came out of the bath and reached for the light switch. "Stop!" said his big sister. "Dry your hands first. Water and electricity don't mix." Kiko dried his hands on his towel and then flicked on the light. "Safety first," he said, pretending to be a superhero with a towel cape.

lessons.title: Light the Bulb
objectives: Build a simple circuit that lights a bulb
Explain why the circuit must be a complete loop
explanation: A circuit is a path that electricity flows around. A simple circuit needs a battery (the power source), wires, and something to power, like a bulb or buzzer.
The circuit must be a complete loop from one end of the battery, through the bulb, and back to the other end. If there is a gap, the electricity stops and the bulb goes out.

A low-voltage battery pack can power this experiment when an adult sets it up. Batteries still need careful handling: keep them out of mouths and away from young children. Never experiment with wall sockets.

vocabulary.meaning: a device that makes a sound

examples: A torch is a simple circuit.
A doorbell circuit with a buzzer.

story.title: The Missing Link
story.text: Zuri connected a battery and a bulb with two wires — but the bulb stayed dark. She traced the path with her finger: battery, wire, bulb, wire... the second wire wasn't touching the battery! She pressed it on, and the bulb glowed. "The loop has to be complete," she said proudly.

lessons.title: Let It Through or Stop It?
objectives: Test materials to sort them into conductors and insulators
Explain why wires are covered in plastic
explanation: A conductor lets electricity flow through it easily. Most metals — copper, iron, aluminium, silver — are good conductors.
An insulator does not let electricity flow easily. Plastic, rubber, wood, glass and cloth are insulators.
Wires have copper inside to carry electricity and a plastic covering outside to keep us safe. Electricians wear rubber gloves for the same reason.

vocabulary.meaning: a material that lets electricity flow

examples: A metal spoon completes the circuit.
A plastic ruler stops it.

story.title: The Conductor Detective
story.text: Ivaan made a circuit with a gap and became a detective. He placed different things in the gap: a metal key — the bulb lit! A pencil eraser — dark. A coin — lit! A plastic button — dark. "Metals are the conductors," he announced. "Everything else is trying to stop the electricity."

lessons.title: Series or Parallel?
objectives: Use a switch to open and close a circuit
Compare series and parallel circuits
explanation: A switch opens (breaks) or closes (completes) a circuit. When the switch is on, the circuit is closed and electricity flows.
In a series circuit, components are connected one after another in a single loop. If one bulb breaks, they all go out, and adding more bulbs makes each one dimmer.
In a parallel circuit, each component has its own path. If one bulb breaks, the others stay lit. Houses are wired in parallel so you can switch lights on and off separately.

vocabulary.meaning: a device that opens or closes a circuit

examples: Old fairy lights where one broken bulb darkens the string (series).
Room lights that work independently (parallel).

story.title: The Diwali Lights Mystery
story.text: Grandpa's old string of Diwali lights wouldn't glow — not a single bulb! Ivaan and Grandpa tested bulbs one by one until they found the broken one. With a new bulb, the whole string sparkled. "Series circuit," said Grandpa. "One breaks, all stop. That's why new lights are often wired differently."

lessons.title: Switch-On Magnets
objectives: Build an electromagnet
Explain how electromagnets differ from permanent magnets
explanation: Magnets attract iron and steel. Every magnet has a north and a south pole: opposite poles attract and like poles repel.
When electricity flows through a coil of wire, it makes a magnetic field. Wrapping the coil around an iron nail makes an electromagnet. More coils or more current make it stronger.
Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet can be switched on and off. Electromagnets are used in scrapyard cranes, electric bells, speakers, motors and MRI scanners in hospitals.

vocabulary.meaning: an object that attracts iron and steel
a magnet made by electricity flowing in a coil

examples: A scrapyard crane lifting cars.
An electric doorbell.

story.title: The Scrapyard Crane
story.text: At the scrapyard, Kiko watched a giant round disc swing over a pile of old cars. The operator pressed a button — CLANG! — a whole car leapt up and stuck to the disc. He moved it over a truck and pressed again. The car dropped. "It's an electromagnet," the operator shouted. "On, it grabs. Off, it lets go!"

lessons.title: Ohm's Law
objectives: Define voltage, current and resistance with units
Use Ohm's law V = I × R in calculations
prerequisites: Can build series and parallel circuits
explanation: Current (I) is the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (amps, A) with an ammeter. Voltage (V) is the "push" that drives the current, measured in volts with a voltmeter. Resistance (R) is how much a component opposes the current, measured in ohms (Ω).
Ohm's law, named after Georg Ohm (1827), says V = I × R for many conductors. If a 6 V battery drives current through a 3 Ω resistor, I = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 A.
A water analogy helps: voltage is like water pressure, current like the flow rate, and resistance like a narrow pipe. Power (watts) = V × I tells how fast energy is used.
examples: A 1.5 V AA battery.
A 230 V household supply in India.

story.title: The Water Pipe Model
story.text: To explain circuits, Meera's teacher used a water tank and pipes. Raising the tank (more pressure) made water flow faster — like more voltage. Squeezing the pipe (more resistance) slowed it. "So a dim bulb in a long series circuit is like a pipe with lots of narrow bits," Meera said. "Exactly!"

lessons.title: Where Electricity Comes From
objectives: Explain how a generator produces electricity
Compare energy sources for power generation
explanation: In 1831, Michael Faraday discovered that moving a magnet near a coil of wire produces electricity — electromagnetic induction. Generators in power stations spin coils within magnetic fields using turbines.

Turbines can be turned by steam (from burning coal or gas, or from nuclear fission), by falling water (hydroelectric), or by wind. Solar panels work differently: photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electricity.
Coal has long been India's largest source of electricity, but solar and wind capacity have grown rapidly. Each source has trade-offs in cost, reliability, pollution and land use.

vocabulary.meaning: a machine that converts motion into electricity

producing electricity by moving magnets and coils

examples: Bhakra Nangal Dam generating hydroelectric power.
Rooftop solar panels on homes.

story.title: Faraday's Coil
story.text: In 1831, Michael Faraday, a bookbinder's apprentice turned scientist, moved a magnet in and out of a coil of wire connected to a meter. The needle flickered! He had made electricity from motion. When asked what use it was, he is said to have replied, "What use is a newborn baby?" Today almost all our electricity relies on his discovery.

lessons.title: Resistors, Diodes and Transistors
objectives: Explain the function of resistors, LEDs, diodes and transistors
Design a simple electronic circuit
explanation: A resistor limits current — for example, protecting an LED from too much current. Resistors are marked with coloured bands showing their value.

A diode lets current flow in one direction only. An LED (light-emitting diode) is a diode that glows; it uses far less energy than old filament bulbs. India's UJALA programme distributed hundreds of millions of LED bulbs to save energy.

A transistor acts as an electronic switch or amplifier: a small current at one terminal controls a larger current. Invented at Bell Labs in 1947, transistors are the basis of all modern computers — billions fit on a single chip.

vocabulary.meaning: a component allowing current one way only

examples: A night light that switches on in the dark using a light sensor and transistor.
A resistor protecting an LED.

story.title: The Night Light
story.text: Kiko wanted a light that turned on by itself at night. He built a circuit with a light-dependent resistor, a transistor and an LED. In daylight, nothing happened. When he covered the sensor with his hand — the LED glowed! "The transistor is the brain," he said. "It decides when to switch on."

lessons.title: From Power Station to Plug
objectives: Explain how transformers and high voltage reduce transmission losses
Calculate energy use in kilowatt-hours
explanation: Power stations are often far from cities. Electricity is sent through transmission lines at very high voltages (hundreds of thousands of volts) because a higher voltage means a lower current for the same power, so less energy is lost as heat. Step-down transformers then reduce the voltage to 230 V for homes.
Energy use is measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh), the "units" on an electricity bill. A 1,000 W (1 kW) heater running for 2 hours uses 2 kWh.
Grid operators must balance supply and demand every second. India's national grid connects all regions; solar power peaks at midday, so storage, flexible demand and other sources help balance it.

vocabulary.meaning: the energy used by 1 kW for one hour
a network of power lines and stations

examples: Tall pylons carrying high-voltage lines.
An electricity bill showing units used.

story.title: The Midday Surplus
story.text: On sunny days, solar farms in Rajasthan pour electricity into the grid at noon, sometimes more than needed nearby. Grid engineers in control rooms shift power to other regions, signal hydro plants to slow down and charge large batteries. At sunset, as solar fades and people switch on lights, they reverse the dance.

lessons.title: Alternating and Direct Current
objectives: Compare AC and DC and their uses
Explain the significance of Maxwell's equations
explanation: Direct current (DC) flows in one direction — from batteries and solar cells. Alternating current (AC) reverses direction many times a second; India's mains supply is 50 Hz, reversing 100 times per second.

In the 1880s "war of the currents", Thomas Edison promoted DC while Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse promoted AC. AC won for grids because transformers can easily change its voltage. Today, high-voltage DC (HVDC) links are used for some very long-distance transmission.

In the 1860s, James Clerk Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism in four equations and predicted that light is an electromagnetic wave. Radio, Wi-Fi, X-rays and visible light are all parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Jagadish Chandra Bose demonstrated millimetre-wave radio communication in Kolkata in the 1890s.

vocabulary.meaning: how many cycles happen each second

examples: A phone charger converting AC to DC.
HVDC lines carrying power across long distances.

story.title: Bose's Invisible Signal
story.text: In 1895, at the Town Hall in Kolkata, Jagadish Chandra Bose used invisible electromagnetic waves to ring a bell and set off a small explosion in another room, through walls. His pioneering work on microwaves and detectors was later recognised by engineers as foundational to radio and wireless technology.

lessons.title: Silicon and a Cleaner Grid
objectives: Explain how semiconductors and integrated circuits work
Evaluate strategies for decarbonising electricity
explanation: Semiconductors like silicon conduct electricity better than insulators but worse than metals. Adding tiny amounts of other elements (doping) creates n-type and p-type regions; their junctions make diodes and transistors. An integrated circuit (microchip) puts billions of tiny transistors on one piece of silicon.

Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling regularly — later stated as about every two years. Chipmaking requires extraordinarily precise factories (fabs); India has announced semiconductor manufacturing projects to build domestic capability.

Decarbonising electricity means shifting from fossil fuels to low-carbon sources while keeping supply reliable. Strategies include solar, wind, hydro and nuclear power, batteries and pumped storage, stronger grids and energy efficiency. India has set a target of net-zero emissions by 2070.

vocabulary.meaning: a material with conductivity between conductors and insulators
adding impurities to change a semiconductor's properties
many components on a single chip

examples: A smartphone processor with billions of transistors.
Pumped storage hydro storing energy for night-time.

story.title: Grains of Sand, Billions of Switches
story.text: Silicon comes from sand. In a fab, purified silicon wafers are patterned with light, layer by layer, in rooms far cleaner than a hospital operating theatre. A single speck of dust can ruin a chip. The result: a sliver smaller than a fingernail containing billions of switches — the brain of every phone and computer.
